passage: I'm Sarita, and I still think about the Tuesday afternoons in Class 9 when Himani ma'am stayed back after school to go through my English essays. She never asked for anything. No gift, no favour, no promise that I'd join her club. When I tried to thank her once, she just said, "Do the same for someone one day." For a long time I thought she was always right. When she suggested I take arts, I almost nodded on reflex. But I loved science, and one afternoon I told her, my heart pounding. She was quiet, then said, "Good. Tell me why." I'm now helping two juniors with their essays. Thanking her was easy. Disagreeing with her was harder, and taught me more.

qa.q: On which afternoons did Himani ma'am stay back to help Sarita?
Why did Sarita almost nod on reflex when Himani ma'am suggested arts?
qa.a: Because she had come to think her mentor was always right. She loved science, though, and her pounding heart shows how hard it was to say so.

qa.q: What could Sarita do to show gratitude for what Himani gave her?
qa.a: Thank her and pass it on, as Himani asked, which Sarita does by helping two juniors with their essays. 🙂

qa.q: How might Himani ma'am have felt when Sarita told her she preferred science?
qa.a: Probably pleased. She stayed quiet, then said, "Good. Tell me why," which suggests she welcomed Sarita thinking for herself.

grounding: A mentor gave time freely; the protagonist thanks her, passes it on and learns she can still disagree.

passage:
You asked me who changed my life at school? I'm Pallavi, and it was Nilesh sir, our librarian.
In Class 8 I was failing English. He noticed me hiding in the library at lunch. Instead of sending me out, he handed me a thin detective novel. "Tell me who did it by Friday, young lady." I did. Then he gave me another. For two years he gave up his lunch breaks to talk about books with me. He never asked for anything.
I thanked him last month, on his retirement day. I gave him a card and cried like a baby.
But here's something funny. Last year, I told him I thought one of his favourite books was boring. He laughed and said, "Good! Argue with me." I think that's the real gift: he never wanted me to agree with everything.
Now I spend Thursday lunches in the library with two Class 7 kids. Detective novels, obviously.

qa.q: What kind of novel did Nilesh sir first give Pallavi?
How does Pallavi feel about Nilesh sir?
qa.a: She feels deep gratitude and affection, enough to cry when she thanked him on his retirement day.

qa.q: How is Pallavi passing on what she received?
qa.a: She spends Thursday lunches in the library with two Class 7 students, sharing detective novels as he did with her.

qa.q: How did Nilesh sir react when Pallavi disagreed with him?
qa.a: He laughed and encouraged her to argue, showing he valued her thinking for herself.

grounding: A teen thanks a mentor who gave time freely, passes it on to younger students, and stays free to disagree with him.

passage:
January. Every Sunday that winter, Suraj bhaiya from the next building taught Rafiq to code on an old laptop. He never took money. "Someone did this for me," he said. Rafiq thought he was the smartest person alive.
March. Rafiq's website for the school fair won second prize. He took Suraj bhaiya a box of jalebis and said, "Thank you, bhaiya. Really." Suraj laughed and shared them with the whole stairwell.
June. Suraj bhaiya suggested a shortcut for the new project. Rafiq thought about it and said, carefully, "I think it'll break on phones." Suraj frowned, checked, then grinned. "You're right. Good." Rafiq felt a strange pride: he could admire someone and still disagree.
August. Two boys from the ground floor asked Rafiq if he could teach them. He set up the old laptop on the stairwell landing. "Someone did this for me," he said.

qa.q: What did Rafiq take to Suraj bhaiya in March?
How did Rafiq feel when he disagreed with Suraj bhaiya in June?
qa.a: He felt nervous at first, then a strange pride at being able to admire someone and still disagree.

qa.q: How does Rafiq show his gratitude over time?
qa.a: He thanks Suraj bhaiya in person and, by August, passes the gift on by teaching two younger boys.

qa.q: How does Suraj bhaiya react to being corrected?
qa.a: He frowns, checks, then grins and admits Rafiq is right, showing he welcomes disagreement.

grounding: A teen grateful to a mentor who taught him freely thanks him, learns to disagree, and passes the gift on.
